caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: CRCNS:v4-2
attempts.entry_title: Crowding in macaque V1 and V4 populations (Henry and Kohn 2022)
attempts.summary: Most of the paper's main findings held up in direction in this data: distractors impair orientation discriminability more in V4 than in V1 for single neurons and populations, modulate V4 responses more strongly, and reduce noise correlations and Fano factors. The size of the crowding effect did not hold: the V4 threshold elevation was 7.30 against the paper's 2.52 at the closest spacing, and V1 values were also higher, with decoder settings the paper does not give. The tuning model's terms, the lower tuning correlation in V4 and the fixed decoder's failure to generalize in V4 held in direction with different values. Whether V4 receptive fields are larger could not be tested, as the mapping data are not deposited.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Henry and Kohn (2022) on CRCNS data set v4-2, which holds the spike counts of the V1 and V4 populations recorded in two macaques viewing target gratings alone and amid distractors (11 sessions of the spacing experiment, 4 of the distractor-orientation experiment). It covers single-neuron and population discriminability, threshold elevation, noise correlations, Fano factors, response modulation, the additive and multiplicative tuning model, tuning correlations and fixed decoders. The receptive-field maps and waveforms are not in the data set.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Henry and Kohn (2022) from CRCNS v4-2
Pseudo-population decoding (Figure S3) from CRCNS v4-2

outcomes.statement: Eleven sessions gave 22 neuronal populations in each area, of on average 19 +/- 1.9 V1 neurons and 31 +/- 3.4 V4 neurons, 396 V1 and 691 V4 neurons in the single-neuron analyses.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 4 (before "Distractors limit target discriminability"); Results, Distractors limit target discriminability, paragraph 1; Figure 3D and 3E (n)
outcomes.quote: We recorded in 11 sessions, yielding 22 neuronal populations in each area. The size of V1 populations was on average 19 ± 1.9 neurons, and the size of V4 populations was 31 ± 3.4 neurons.
outcomes.notes: The data set holds 11 sessions and 22 populations per area, with exactly 396 V1 and 691 V4 units (264 and 132, 288 and 403 per animal, as in Figure S7) and mean population sizes 18.0 +/- 1.7 and 31.4 +/- 3.4, all within tolerance (given as measured). The deposited units are the paper's selected units. The Methods' rule applied to them, with blank epochs as the spontaneous condition, keeps 115 V1 and 147 V4 units under reading (a) and 133 and 174 under reading (b), mean sizes 5.2 to 7.9, outside tolerance. So sessions and populations hold under both readings and the unit counts hold only for the deposit as it is. In 12 of 22 populations per area (sessions 1, 2, 8 to 11) the epochs labelled blank respond like the target epochs, so no unit there can pass the rule.
deviations: Assumed that the spontaneous rate is the count in the blank epochs (target and distractor contrast 0), the only spontaneous data in the files; the Methods do not say how it was measured. The question is recorded for the paper's authors as a methods_unavailable finding.
All later analyses use every deposited unit, since the stated selection does not regenerate the paper's counts and the deposit holds exactly those counts.

outcomes.statement: V4 receptive fields are many-fold larger than V1 receptive fields, and the aggregate receptive field maps of the V1 and V4 populations overlap substantially in each animal.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure 1B
outcomes.quote: As expected, individual V1 receptive fields were small, and the receptive fields of V4 neurons were many-fold larger (Figure 1B, top). Aggregate receptive field maps showed substantial overlap in the visual field representation of recorded V1 and V4 populations in each animal
outcomes.notes: The receptive-field mapping sessions (small gratings on a 9 x 9 degree grid) are not in the data set, which holds only data.zip with the two experiments' spike counts (bucket listing of v4-2/live and its filelist.txt). The paper names no other deposit.

outcomes.statement: V1 single-neuron discriminability of target orientation is lower with the nearest distractors than for targets alone, with a regression slope of 0.60 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.69).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors limit target discriminability, paragraph 2; Figure 2A
outcomes.quote: For V1 neurons, discriminability was better when targets were presented alone ... (Figure 2A), evident as a regression slope that was significantly less than 1 (slope = 0.60, 95% confidence interval

statistics.test: bootstrap over neurons, 95% confidence interval of the regression slope

outcomes.notes: V1 slope at 1.3 degrees 0.580 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.486 to 0.669), within 0.60 +/- 0.10, CI below 1; 0.607 for a fit through (0.5, 0.5); 0.602 with the lower orientation as preferred. Per animal 0.495 (AL) and 0.644 (CA).
deviations: The preferred extreme is the one closer to 0 degrees as an axial orientation (Results, "We assumed the orientation closer to 0 would evoke stronger responses"); for references at 0 degrees, where both are equally close, the lower is taken. In the paper's frame of orientations relative to the reference the extremes are always equally close to 0; taking the lower orientation as preferred throughout changes the Figure 2 slopes by at most 0.022 (0.602 and 0.200 at 1.3 degrees, 0.742 and 0.440 at 2.6), shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: In V4 the loss of single-neuron discriminability with the nearest distractors is stronger, with a regression slope of 0.20 (95% CI 0.14 to 0.26).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors limit target discriminability, paragraph 2; Figure 2B
outcomes.quote: In V4, the loss of discriminability with nearby distractors was stronger (Figure 2B, slope = 0.20, [0.14 0.26])

statistics.test: bootstrap over neurons, 95% confidence interval of the regression slope

outcomes.notes: V4 slope at 1.3 degrees 0.206 (0.145 to 0.269), within 0.20 +/- 0.06; 0.203 through (0.5, 0.5). Per animal 0.319 (AL) and 0.122 (CA).

outcomes.statement: At the farthest spacing the loss of single-neuron discriminability is more moderate, with slopes of 0.74 (0.66 to 0.82) in V1 and 0.44 (0.37 to 0.50) in V4.
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors limit target discriminability, paragraph 2; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: When distractors were moved further from the target, effects on discriminability were slightly more moderate (Figure 2C, farthest spacing, slope = 0.74, [0.66 0.82]) ... and remained pronounced even when distractors were placed farther from the target (Figure 2C, farthest spacing, slope = 0.44, [0.37 0.50])

statistics.test: bootstrap over neurons, 95% confidence interval of the regression slope
bootstrap over neurons, 95% confidence interval of the regression slope

outcomes.statement: Distractors impair single-neuron discriminability more in V4 than in V1 at every target-distractor spacing.
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors limit target discriminability, paragraph 2; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: Thus, distractors led to a greater impairment in single neuron discriminability of targets in V4 than V1, over all spatial scales.
outcomes.notes: V4 slopes 0.206, 0.297, 0.313, 0.437 against V1 0.580, 0.689, 0.641, 0.728 at 1.3 to 2.6 degrees; the 95% CIs do not overlap at any spacing (reading b), and V4 is lower in each animal at every spacing.

outcomes.statement: In one animal at the nearest spacing, V4 population decoding performance with distractors tends to be lower than for targets alone when performance is above chance (p < 0.001), while in V1 the loss is not significant (p > 0.05).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors limit target discriminability, paragraph 4; Figure 2D and 2E
outcomes.quote: In V4, when decoder performance was above chance (Figure 2E, abscissa values greater than 0.5), performance for responses to targets with distractors tended to be lower (ordinate; p < 0.001 for difference; addressed further below). In V1, performance loss was less evident (p > 0.05 for difference

statistics.about: V4, target alone against with nearest distractors
statistics.n: 84 cases (pairings of target stimuli across sessions), one animal

statistics.about: V1, target alone against with nearest distractors

outcomes.notes: Monkey AL has the 84 cases (14 populations x 6 pairs). V4 with target-alone performance above 0.5 (74 cases) - 0.645 alone against 0.536 crowded, paired t p = 1.5e-15, Wilcoxon p = 2.8e-11. V1 over all 84 cases - 0.560 against 0.552, p = 0.46 and 0.60, so the V1 part holds under the unrestricted reading; with the V4 restriction (62 cases) V1 gives p = 0.018 and 0.025. The 5-fold variant and monkey CA give the same pattern. The criterion shows V1 both restricted and unrestricted and asks for one reading, so the outcome rests on the unrestricted V1 test.
deviations: Decoders z-score each unit on the training trials and choose the penalty from 13 values of C (0.01 to 100); neither is stated in the paper (standard choices, in crowding.py).

outcomes.statement: In V1, distractors elevate the estimated discrimination threshold of the populations by 1.31 +/- 0.10 at the closest spacing and 1.15 +/- 0.08 at the farthest, significant at all but the farthest spacing (permutation test, p < 0.05).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors limit target discriminability, paragraph 6; Figure 2F
outcomes.quote: Distractors at the closest spacing yielded the largest threshold elevations, 1.31 ± 0.10; distractors at the farthest spacing yielded the smallest elevation, 1.15 ± 0.08. The estimated threshold elevation was statistically significant for all but the farthest target-distractor separation (permutation test, p < 0.05).

statistics.about: threshold elevation above 1 at 1.3, 1.6 and 2.1 degrees

outcomes.notes: V1 threshold elevation 1.685 +/- 0.351 at 1.3 degrees and 1.669 +/- 0.314 at 2.6 (mean of AL 1.888 and CA 1.483; AL 2.062 and CA 1.277), outside 1.31 +/- 0.10 and 1.15 +/- 0.08. The permutation test gives p < 0.05 only at 2.1 degrees (0.048 and 0.047), not at 1.3 or 1.6 (0.18 to 0.42) or 2.6 (0.059 and 0.062); with 5 folds none. Both trial-count readings give the same estimates, since they differ only in scale of the likelihood, so they are one reading for the estimate. 62 of 84 AL and 34 of 48 CA points have target-alone performance above 0.5 and enter the fit. With no crowding (true k = 1, binomial draws around the recorded performances) the estimate is biased upward, mean 1.17 to 1.18 in V1 (95th percentile 1.26 to 1.29), and the permutation nulls have medians of 1.37 to 1.63; the V1 estimates exceed the calibration but lie near their null medians (1.63 at 1.3 degrees, 1.49 at 2.6). The null is shifted much further than the calibration, so it is not calibrated by it; against the calibration every V1 estimate would count as elevated, against the null only 2.1 degrees does. The significance pattern therefore says little either way, and the outcome rests on the values. With each decoder that has no nonzero coefficient replaced by the nearest one that has one, V1 gives 1.688 and 1.575, also outside, with the same significance pattern.
deviations: The binomial trial count is read as (a) the held-out trials of one fold and (b) all trials of the pair; the maximum-likelihood k is the same under both, and only the bootstrap and permutation draws differ.

The paper's code is not public; the decoder's standardisation and penalty grid and the k grid (0.2 to 20) are standard choices that could change the estimates. Under the paper's penalty rule the chosen penalty leaves no nonzero coefficient in 9.9% to 14.5% of V1 and 4.8% to 18.4% of V4 outer folds, where the decoder predicts one class; how often depends on the grid's lower bound (C = 0.01). Replacing these decoders changes mean performances by at most 0.007 and the estimates little (variant in the notebook).

outcomes.statement: In V4 the estimated threshold elevations are greater than in V1, 2.52 +/- 0.23 for the closest distractors and 1.89 +/- 0.19 for the farthest, significant at all spacings (permutation test, p < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors limit target discriminability, paragraph 6; Figure 2F
outcomes.quote: In V4 populations, the estimated threshold elevations were greater than those in V1 (Figure 2F, red): 2.52 ± 0.23 for the closest distractors and 1.89 ± 0.19 for the farthest distractors (significant for all distractor separations, permutation test, p < 0.001).
outcomes.notes: V4 7.302 +/- 2.465 at 1.3 degrees and 2.607 +/- 0.289 at 2.6, against 2.52 +/- 0.23 and 1.89 +/- 0.19; permutation p = 0.001 (the smallest attainable) at all four spacings and V4 above V1 at every spacing. So the elevation is greater in V4 and significant, but three times the paper's value at 1.3 degrees. The CA estimates are 10.87 and 18.52 at 1.3 and 1.6 degrees, and 10.87 and 18.47 on a grid up to 1000, so the grid bound of 20 does not censor the main run (in the 5-fold run CA at 1.6 degrees reaches it, 41.0 on the wider grid); AL gives 3.74 and 1.83 at 1.3 and 2.6. With 5 folds 10.17 and 3.04. The permutation null medians are 3.51 and 1.75 at 1.3 and 2.6 degrees. With each decoder that has no nonzero coefficient replaced by the nearest one that has one, V4 gives 6.91 and 2.55 and CA 10.46 at 1.3 degrees (20, the grid bound, at 1.6), so these decoders do not explain the large CA estimates.

outcomes.statement: Pseudo-populations built by combining neurons across sessions give a broader range of decoding performance and similar estimates of threshold elevation.
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors limit target discriminability, paragraph 7; Figure S3
outcomes.quote: Pseudo-populations provided a broader range of performance values and yielded similar estimates of how distractors affected thresholds (Figure S3).
outcomes.notes: With 20 draws per size, pseudo-populations give a broader range of target-alone performance (V1 0.343 to 1.000, SD 0.170; V4 0.370 to 1.000, SD 0.173) than recorded populations (0.395 to 0.973 and 0.420 to 0.963, SD 0.117 and 0.123). Their threshold elevations lie within twice the recorded SEM at 7 of 8 area and spacing pairs; V4 at 1.6 degrees is 3.50 against 10.35 +/- 2.45. The closest pass is V1 at 2.6 degrees, 1.15 against 1.67 +/- 0.32 (difference 0.52, margin 0.63). The comparison is with this attempt's recorded estimates, which differ from the paper's (fig2f claims). The pseudo-population V1 value at 2.6 degrees (1.15) is the paper's 1.15; at 1.3 degrees (1.64) it is not near 1.31.
deviations: 20 draws per size, the claims file's standard choice; the estimate is pooled over all draws (480 points per area and spacing). Only the held-out trial count is used, as both counts give the same k.

Each population contributes, per draw, a random subset of its trials of each stimulus, as many as the smallest count over populations (19 to 24), the same trials for all its units; trials are matched by index across populations.

outcomes.statement: Distractors reduce noise correlations, from 0.07 +/- 0.003 to 0.05 +/- 0.002 in V1 and from 0.11 +/- 0.001 to 0.06 +/- 0.001 in V4 with the nearest distractors (paired t test, p < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors modulate neuronal responsivity and variability, paragraph 2; Figure 3A and 3B
outcomes.quote: In V1 (Figure 3A; see Figure S1 for sample responses), pairwise correlations decreased from 0.07 ± 0.003 for targets alone to 0.05 ± 0.002 with the nearest distractors (paired t test, p < 0.001). In V4 (Figure 3B), the corresponding decrease in correlations was from 0.11 ± 0.001 to 0.06 ± 0.001 (paired t test, p < 0.001).

statistics.about: V1, targets alone against nearest distractors
V4, targets alone against nearest distractors

outcomes.notes: Mean rSC from 0.0672 +/- 0.0025 to 0.0479 +/- 0.0023 in V1 and from 0.1122 +/- 0.0013 to 0.0555 +/- 0.0010 in V4 with the nearest distractors; paired t p = 2e-21 (V1) and below 1e-300 (V4). 4036 and 13101 pairs. The decrease holds in each animal (V1 AL 0.034 to 0.030, CA 0.152 to 0.092; V4 AL 0.066 to 0.050, CA 0.127 to 0.057).
deviations: Only reading (a), every stored epoch as a presentation, could be run; the files do not mark which epoch of a trial came first, and the residuals do not reveal the pairing.

outcomes.statement: When decoders are fit to trial-shuffled responses, distractors still lead to threshold elevations similar to those in the original data, so the change in correlations plays a minimal role in the information loss.
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors modulate neuronal responsivity and variability, paragraph 2; Figure 3C
outcomes.quote: In these shuffled data, distractors led to threshold elevations similar to those seen in the original data (Figure 3C), indicating changes in correlations, although substantial, played a minimal role in the information loss we observed.
outcomes.notes: Under both readings (all trials shuffled, or training trials only) and both trial counts, the shuffled estimates lie within twice the bootstrap SEM of the original at 8 of 8 area and spacing pairs (for example V4 at 1.3 degrees 8.40 and 9.64 against 7.30 +/- 2.47), and V4 exceeds V1 at every spacing. The originals are this attempt's estimates, which differ from the paper's values (fig2f claims). The test is lenient where the SEMs are large (V4 2.0 to 2.5 at 1.3 to 2.1 degrees).

outcomes.statement: In V1, distractors at the closest spacing slightly reduce variability, the Fano factor falling from 1.05 +/- 0.02 for targets alone to 0.98 +/- 0.01 (paired t test, p < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors modulate neuronal responsivity and variability, paragraph 3; Figure 3D
outcomes.quote: In V1, distractors at the closest spacing led to a slight reduction in variability (Figure 3D, from 1.05 ± 0.02 for targets alone to 0.98 ± 0.01, paired t test, p < 0.001).
outcomes.notes: Geometric mean Fano factor 1.051 alone and 0.985 at 1.3 degrees; paired t p = 3.3e-08 on Fano factors and 1.4e-07 on logs. No neuron or condition had to be dropped.

outcomes.statement: In V4, distractors at all spacings significantly reduce variability, the Fano factor falling from 1.00 +/- 0.01 for targets alone to 0.93 +/- 0.01 with the closest distractors (paired t test, p < 0.001 for each spacing).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors modulate neuronal responsivity and variability, paragraph 3; Figure 3E
outcomes.quote: In V4, distractors at all spacings led to a significant reduction in variability (Figure 3E, 1.00 ± 0.01 for targets alone to 0.93 ± 0.01 with closest distractors, paired t test, p < 0.001 for each spacing).
outcomes.notes: V4 0.997 alone and 0.928 at 1.3 degrees; the decrease has p < 0.001 at all four spacings (largest 1.4e-09 on Fano factors, 8.7e-09 on logs).

outcomes.statement: In V1, distractors at the closest spacing suppress and facilitate responses in roughly equal proportion, with significant suppression in 23% and facilitation in 27% of neurons; for farther distractors modulation is weaker, with 2.5% significant facilitation and 13% suppression.
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors modulate neuronal responsivity and variability, paragraph 4; Figure 4A
outcomes.quote: For distractors at the closest spacing, suppression and facilitation occurred in roughly equal proportion (Figure 4A, dark blue). ... Suppressive effects were statistically significant in 23% of neurons (permutation test, p < 0.05); facilitation was significant in 27% cases. ... modulation was weaker; only 2.5% cases of significant facilitation were observed (the expected false positive rate) and 13% cases of suppression.
outcomes.notes: Two-sided rule, pooling within orientation (first readings, given as measured) - at 1.3 degrees 24.5% suppressed and 26.5% facilitated, both within tolerance (pooling over all 24.7% and 26.0%); 56.6% of indices below 1. At 2.6 degrees 2.0% facilitated and 14.4% suppressed, both outside 2.25 to 2.75 and 11.7 to 14.3 (pooling over all 1.8%, outside, and 12.9%, within). One-sided at 2.6 degrees gives 2.5% facilitation but 19.7% suppression, and the one-sided closest pair (28.8% and 28.3%) is out. Pooled over the three farther spacings facilitation is 4.0 to 5.1%. The closest-spacing pair holds and the far pair does not, the criterion's partial case. At 2.6 degrees 2.0% is 8 of 396 neurons and 14.4% is 57, against 9 or 10 and 47 to 56 allowed, so each value misses by one neuron; the 0.25-point tolerance is finer than the counts resolve, which is asked of a reader (questions/henry-2022.yaml). No null draw is undefined in V1.

outcomes.statement: For the closest distractors most V4 neurons are facilitated (mean index 1.11 +/- 0.38, t test, p < 0.001; significant facilitation in 51% and suppression in 14% of cases), and the average index is larger than in V1 (one-sided t test, p < 0.01); at larger spacing facilitation and suppression are roughly equal (0.97 +/- 0.48; 24% and 32% significant).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors modulate neuronal responsivity and variability, paragraph 5; Figure 4B
outcomes.quote: For the closest distractors, most V4 neurons showed facilitation (Figure 4B, dark red points, 1.11 ± 0.38, t test, p < 0.001; 51% of cases of facilitation were statistically significant and 14% of suppressive cases) and the average modulation index was larger than in V1 (one-sided t test, p < 0.01). As distractor spacing increased, a roughly equal proportion of V4 neurons exhibited facilitation and suppression (Figure 4B, light red points, 0.97 ± 0.48; 24% and 32% cases involved significant facilitation and suppression, respectively).

statistics.about: V4 mean modulation index against 1, closest spacing
V4 against V1 mean modulation index, closest spacing

outcomes.notes: Under the two-sided rule, percentages of all neurons and the farthest spacing, all six values are within tolerance under both poolings; mean index 1.134 (SD 0.379, the paper's 0.38), 69.8% above 1, p = 1.9e-19 against 1; far mean 1.009 (SD 0.473). V4 against V1 at 1.3 degrees, one-sided, p = 0.009 on log indices and p = 0.074 on the indices (V1 mean 1.097), so the comparison holds only on logs, a reading the criterion lists. With percentages of the facilitated and suppressed neurons the values are far out (72.6% and 49.8%).

outcomes.statement: The strength of modulation, the mean absolute log modulation index, is significant in both areas at all spacings (permutation test, p < 0.01).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors modulate neuronal responsivity and variability, paragraph 6; Figure 4C
outcomes.quote: To quantify the strength of modulation by distractors, regardless of whether it facilitated or suppressed responsivity, we averaged the absolute value of each neuron’s modulation index (log-transformed). The modulation in both areas was statistically significant, for all target-distractor spacings (permutation test, p < 0.01).
outcomes.notes: Observed strength 0.087 to 0.285 against a null 99th percentile of 0.071 to 0.074 at all eight area and spacing pairs, under both poolings; p = 0.001 in each, the smallest attainable.

outcomes.statement: Modulation strength is stronger in V4 than in V1 at all separations (one-sided t test, p = 0.01 for the closest distractors, p < 0.001 for the others).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors modulate neuronal responsivity and variability, paragraph 6; Figure 4C
outcomes.quote: The average modulation was stronger in V4 than in V1 at all separations (Figure 4C, one-sided t test, p = 0.01 for

outcomes.statement: Modulation strength in V4 is largely maintained across spacings (one-sided t test nearest against farthest, p = 0.44), whereas in V1 the farthest separation yields weaker modulation than the nearest (one-sided t test, p < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors modulate neuronal responsivity and variability, paragraph 6; Figure 4C
outcomes.quote: Furthermore, modulation strength in V4 was largely maintained across target-distractor spacings (p = 0.44, one-sided t test comparing nearest to farthest distractors), whereas the farthest separation yielded weaker modulation in V1 than the nearest separation (one-sided t test, p < 0.001).
outcomes.notes: V4 nearest 0.2854 against farthest 0.2813 (difference 0.0041), one-sided p = 0.403 paired and 0.409 two-sample (paper 0.44); V1 0.2426 against 0.0866, p = 9.3e-23 paired and 2.5e-22 two-sample.

outcomes.statement: Whether distractors suppress or facilitate responses depends on the alignment of the receptive field with the target; V1 neurons driven by the target alone are suppressed, most by near distractors, no V4 neuron is driven by the target alone, and neurons whose receptive fields straddle target and distractors are facilitated by near and suppressed by far distractors in both areas.
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors modulate neuronal responsivity and variability, paragraph 4; Figure S4
outcomes.quote: Whether distractors suppressed or facilitated responses was related to the alignment of the receptive field with the target stimulus (Figure S4).
outcomes.notes: The coarse mapping at the start of each session (targets and each distractor shown alone) is not in the data set. The files hold distractor-only epochs, but with all four distractors together, so the per-distractor responses the Figure S4 classes need cannot be formed.

outcomes.statement: Fitting either a multiplicative or an additive change of target tuning alone, neurons facilitated by distractors are better described by the additive model and suppressed neurons by the multiplicative model, in V1 and V4; each single form reduces discriminability, but less than in the measured responses.
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors modulate neuronal responsivity and variability, paragraph 8; Figure S5
outcomes.quote: In prior work,21 we had found that V1 neurons whose responses were suppressed were better described by the multiplicative model, whereas those that were facilitated by distractors were better described by an additive model. In the V1 and V4 responses reported here, we observed a similar outcome (Figure S5).
outcomes.notes: In the tuning model's cases 89.8% (V1) and 97.0% (V4) of facilitated cases favour the additive model and 83.7% and 92.1% of suppressed cases the multiplicative one (all neurons 86.1%, 92.2%, 81.0%, 88.5%). The single-form simulation gives slopes 0.826 to 0.911 (V1) and 0.776 to 0.822 (V4) with recorded trial counts, below 1 as point slopes and above the measured Figure 2 slopes at 4 of 4 spacings in each area; judged by the upper CI instead, V1 at 2.6 degrees reaches 1.001. On the random-split selection the shares are 93.1%, 98.0%, 84.9% and 93.2% and the slopes 0.807 to 0.887, above the measured ones at 4 of 4.
deviations: The selection is the tuning model's (reliability above 0.5), as the criterion reads it, so the V4 cases inherit the different even/odd split (see fig5bc-tuning-model-terms).

outcomes.statement: With both terms allowed, V1 tuning amid distractors has a multiplicative term below 1 (0.59 +/- 0.03) and a positive additive term (0.39 +/- 0.16); in V4 the multiplicative term is 0.36 +/- 0.01 and the additive term 0.90 +/- 0.02; the multiplicative term is smaller and the additive term larger in V4 than in V1 (t test).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors modulate neuronal responsivity and variability, paragraph 9; Figure 5B and 5C
outcomes.quote: For V1 neurons (Figure 5B), the amplitude of the multiplicative term was significantly less than 1 on average (abscissa, 0.59 ± 0.03), indicating a compression of the tuning curve, and the additive term was positive (0.39 ± 0.16), indicating an upward translation of the tuning. For V4 neurons (Figure 5C), the amplitude of the multiplicative term was also less than 1 (0.36 ± 0.01) and the additive term was positive (0.90 ± 0.02). The multiplicative term for V4 neurons was significantly smaller than for V1 neurons (t test, p < 0.001) and the additive term was significantly larger for V4 than V1 (t test, p > 0.001).
outcomes.notes: The criterion keeps 146 V1 neurons, exactly the paper's (89 and 57 per animal), and 244 V4 against 198 (114 and 130 against 93 and 105). Single random half splits keep 238.3 V4 neurons on average (219 to 256 over 20 splits) and 143.8 V1 neurons (126 to 163), so the stored-order counts lie in the range of random splits and the V4 order does not explain the excess. m is below 1 in both areas (p < 1e-35), V4 has the smaller m (-0.251, p = 3.6e-18) and the larger a (+0.312, p = 3.7e-18). Only the V4 additive term is within tolerance; V1 m 0.405 and a 0.596 against 0.59 and 0.39, V4 m 0.154 against 0.36. Fits on single trials and on means, and means over cases or neurons, agree within 0.001. The effect is present with different values, so partially reproduced. On the selection by reliability averaged over 20 random splits (109 V1, 160 V4 neurons) m is 0.403 and 0.178 and a 0.588 and 0.894, again only the V4 additive term within tolerance, with the V4 differences at p = 4.1e-16 and 1.9e-14; the outcome is the same.
deviations: Even and odd presentations follow the stored order of the epochs. The V4 epochs are not stored in recording order (data check), so the V4 split cannot be the paper's; it counts as a random half split, and single random splits keep as many neurons. The tuning-model claims are repeated on a selection by reliability averaged over 20 random half splits as a variant.

outcomes.statement: In the neurons fitted with the tuning model, the fit quality (a normalized likelihood between a null model at 0 and an oracle at 1) is 0.63 in V1 and 0.73 in V4.
outcomes.source: STAR Methods, Quantification and statistical analysis, the paragraph beginning "We assessed how the target orientation tuning of each neuron changed"
outcomes.quote: In these neurons, the fit quality was 0.63 and 0.73 in V1 and V4, respectively, where the fit quality was defined as a normalized likelihood, between a ‘null’ model which predicts the response to be the mean across all stimuli (a value of 0) and an ‘oracle’ model which predicts the measured response (a value of 1).
outcomes.notes: Mean per case 0.455 (V1) and 0.410 (V4), given as measured; median 0.460 and 0.328; pooled 0.623 and 0.589. V1 pooled is within 0.63 +/- 0.063, but no reading puts V4 within 0.73 +/- 0.073. On the random-split selection V4 gives 0.440, 0.410 and 0.651, also outside.

outcomes.statement: In both V1 and V4 the additive and multiplicative terms covary strongly, consistent with a flattening of tuning with maintained responsivity.
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors modulate neuronal responsivity and variability, paragraph 10; Figure 5B and 5C
outcomes.quote: In both V1 and V4, there was a strong covariation between the additive and multiplicative terms, consistent with a flattening of the tuning function with maintained responsivity.
outcomes.notes: Pearson r = -0.892 (V1, 584 cases) and -0.682 (V4, 976 cases), p < 1e-130; Spearman -0.955 and -0.839. Over 20 single random half splits, each keeping the neurons whose reliability on that split is above 0.5, r is -0.966 to -0.854 in V1 and -0.893 to -0.639 in V4 (medians -0.886 and -0.683), so the criterion holds on all 20 and the stored-order split is typical. On the selection by reliability averaged over 20 random splits V1 gives r = -0.913 but V4 r = -0.459 (p = 1.1e-34), below the criterion's 0.5, which would make the outcome partial.
deviations: Assumed that the tuning-model selection is the even/odd split in stored order, whose counts match those of single random half splits in both areas (V1 146 against 143.8, V4 244 against 238.3) and whose V4 r is at the median of 20 single random splits (-0.682 against -0.683, all 20 meet the criterion), over a selection by reliability averaged over 20 random splits, which the paper does not describe. Under that variant V4 r is -0.459 and the outcome would be partial. Asked of the paper's authors in the methods_unavailable finding.

outcomes.statement: Some fits give a negative multiplicative term, offset by a large additive term; such cases are rare in V1 and more frequent in V4.
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors modulate neuronal responsivity and variability, paragraph 12 (the last before "Distractors alter neuronal tuning for target orientation"); Figure 5B and 5C
outcomes.quote: We note that the model fitting revealed cases in which the multiplicative term was negative; as a result, a large additive term was required to offset the negative responses and reproduce the firing rate. These cases occurred rarely in V1 but more often in V4
outcomes.notes: m < 0 in 23.3% of V1 and 35.1% of V4 cases (Fisher p = 7.7e-07); mean a with m < 0 is 1.29 and 1.41 against 0.38 and 0.63 otherwise. V4 is more frequent, but the V1 fraction is not below 10%, the criterion's partial case. On the random-split selection 20.2% and 33.6% (Fisher p = 1.3e-06), the same outcome.

outcomes.statement: Simulating crowded responses with the fitted multiplicative and additive terms yields some loss of discriminability in V1 and more in V4, similar to but slightly stronger than the measured loss, and depending weakly on spacing.
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors modulate neuronal responsivity and variability, paragraph 11; Figure 5D and 5E
outcomes.quote: This simulation yielded some loss of discriminability in V1 (Figure 5D) and more substantial effects in V4 (Figure 5E); the effects in simulations were similar but slightly stronger than the losses observed in the measured responses (Figure 2). In both areas, the loss of discriminability depended weakly on target-distractor spacing, as in the data.
outcomes.notes: With recorded trial counts and the Figure 2C slopes over all neurons (readings a and a), simulated V4 slopes 0.243 to 0.336 are below V1 0.404 to 0.567 at every spacing, and the simulated slope is at or below the measured one at 4 of 4 spacings in V1 and 3 of 4 in V4. With 1000 trials V4 meets this at only 1 of 4 spacings against all neurons (3 of 4 against the fitted neurons). With recorded trial counts against the fitted neurons' own slopes the criterion is met as well (4 of 4 in each area). The claim's "similar" and "weakly on spacing" are not tested by the criterion. Reading (a, a) is near its limit; over 20 single random half splits it holds on 11 (V4 at or below at 2 of 4 on 9 splits), and the stored-order split with another simulation draw gives V4 2 of 4. Against the fitted neurons' own slopes with recorded trial counts it holds on all 20 single random splits. On the selection by reliability averaged over 20 random splits the simulated V4 slope is at or below the measured one over all neurons at only 1 of 4 spacings (2 of 4 with another draw), which would fail reading (a, a), but at 4 of 4 against the selected neurons' own slopes, which meets the criterion. So under the reading against the fitted neurons' slopes the outcome holds on every selection tested; it stays marked as assumed, as verified.
deviations: Assumed that the tuning-model selection is the even/odd split in stored order, whose counts match those of single random half splits in both areas, over a selection by reliability averaged over 20 random splits, which the paper does not describe; under that variant V4 meets the comparison against all neurons at 1 of 4 spacings, and against the selected neurons' own slopes at 4 of 4. Asked of the paper's authors in the methods_unavailable finding.

outcomes.statement: Tuning for targets alone correlates well with tuning for targets with nearby distractors in V1 (0.38 +/- 0.03 for cells above a reliability criterion of 0.5), and significantly less in V4 (0.22 +/- 0.03; one-sided t test, p < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors alter neuronal tuning for target orientation, paragraph 2; Figure 6C
outcomes.quote: For instance, for cells exceeding a criterion of 0.5, the correlation between tuning with and without distractors was 0.38 ± 0.03. Tuning correlation was significantly lower in V4 neurons (Figure 6C, red points), with the corresponding value being 0.22 ± 0.03 (p < 0.001 for comparison with V1, one-sided t test).
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), criterion 0.5 - V1 0.389 +/- 0.042 (within) and V4 0.161 +/- 0.039 (below 0.22 +/- 0.03), p = 8.9e-05; reading (b) - V1 0.460 (out) and V4 0.238 (within), p = 1.2e-04. V4 is lower than V1 at every criterion (p = 5.9e-05 at 0.7, 0.009 at 0.9). No reading gives both values; V4 is lower than the paper's value, a larger effect. The V4 selection rests on a split that is not the paper's (fig5bc-tuning-model-terms); a random-split reliability gives V1 0.413 and V4 0.159.

outcomes.statement: Target tuning with near and with far distractors correlates less in V4 than V1 (0.17 +/- 0.02 against 0.36 +/- 0.02 at criterion 0.5; one-sided t test, p < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors alter neuronal tuning for target orientation, paragraph 3; Figure 6D
outcomes.quote: In this comparison too, correlations between target tuning were lower in V4 than V1 (Figure 6D, for cutoff of 0.5, correlations were 0.17 ± 0.02 and 0.36 ± 0.02, respectively, p < 0.001, one-sided t test).
outcomes.notes: Reading (a) V4 0.135 and V1 0.432, p = 1.2e-06; reading (b) 0.214 and 0.515, p = 1.8e-07. V4 is lower than V1 as claimed, but no value is within 0.17 +/- 0.02 and 0.36 +/- 0.02.

outcomes.statement: In 4 further sessions, target tuning with two distractor configurations whose orientations differ by 20 degrees differs substantially in V4 (correlation 0.24 +/- 0.06) and is nearly unaffected in V1 (0.65 +/- 0.06; p < 0.001, one-sided t test).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors alter neuronal tuning for target orientation, paragraph 3; Figure 6E; STAR Methods, Visual stimuli
outcomes.quote: V4 tuning differed substantially between these two conditions, whereas V1 tuning was nearly unaffected (Figure 6E, for cutoff of 0.5, V4 correlation values were 0.24 ± 0.06 and V1 correlation values were 0.65 ± 0.06, p < 0.001 for difference between areas, one-sided t test).
outcomes.notes: Criterion 0.5 - V4 0.214 +/- 0.047 (90 neurons) and V1 0.644 +/- 0.061 (50 neurons), p = 6.7e-08; also at criteria 0.7 (p = 2.1e-05) and 0.9 (p = 0.006).

outcomes.statement: The changes in tuning of Figure 6 are also evident when the analyses are limited to the best-isolated neurons, those with waveform SNR in the top third.
outcomes.source: STAR Methods, Neurophysiological recording, the paragraph beginning "Extracellular voltage signals"
outcomes.quote: We confirmed that the changes in neuronal tuning shown in Figure 6 were evident when our analyses were limited to the most well-isolated neurons, as defined by those units having a waveform SNR in the top 33th percentile.
outcomes.notes: The files hold spike counts only, with no waveforms or SNR per unit, so the best-isolated third cannot be chosen. No other deposit is named by the paper.

outcomes.statement: Projected onto the decoding axis of the opposite condition, discriminability is largely preserved in V1 (d' 0.95 +/- 0.13 same, 0.88 +/- 0.12 cross, p = 0.20) but drops significantly in V4 (1.02 +/- 0.13 against 0.67 +/- 0.05, p = 0.002, paired t test).
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors alter neuronal tuning for target orientation, paragraph 6; Figure 7C and 7D
outcomes.quote: When data were projected onto the decoding axis of the opposing condition (‘‘cross’’), discriminability was largely preserved in V1 (d-prime of 0.95 ± 0.13 for same projection and 0.88 ± 0.12 for cross projection, p = 0.20, paired t test). In contrast, discriminability dropped significantly for V4 (1.02 ± 0.13 versus 0.67 ± 0.05, p = 0.002, paired t test).
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), all pairs - V1 same 0.354 +/- 0.044 and cross 0.380 +/- 0.039 (22 populations), paired t p = 0.36, no drop; V4 0.411 +/- 0.044 against 0.265 +/- 0.043, p = 0.0004. With the 18 degree pair alone V4 0.710 against 0.467 (p = 0.002) and V1 0.645 against 0.682 (p = 0.50). The tests hold under every reading, the d' values are well below the paper's under every reading, the criterion's partial case. Per population, before averaging, the 18 degree pair gives same-axis d' of 0.02 to 1.66 (V1) and 0.08 to 1.36 (V4); 17 of 22 V1 and 16 of 22 V4 populations are below the paper's means. Only 8 of 440 V1 and 7 of 440 V4 fixed decoders have no nonzero coefficient; replacing them with the nearest decoder that has one changes the per-population means by at most 0.008 and the tests not at all (p = 0.43 and 0.0004).
deviations: Ten folds over all trials of both conditions and all four orientations; in each, both decoders are trained on the extremes of the training trials and all held-out trials are projected. The d' is signed so that the trained direction is positive.

outcomes.statement: The distinct V4 decoding axes for different displays do not arise from relying on distinct subsets of neurons; most target-responsive neurons remain driven with distractors, and the most informative neuron for targets alone remains informative with distractors.
outcomes.source: Results, Distractors alter neuronal tuning for target orientation, paragraph 6; Figure S6
outcomes.quote: In additional analyses, we confirmed that the distinct decoding axes in V4 for different displays do not arise from relying on distinct subsets of neurons (Figure S6).
outcomes.notes: Mean fraction still driven with distractors 0.944 to 0.960 (V1) and 0.866 to 0.953 (V4), at least 0.8 at every spacing; the top unit's normalized d' alone correlates with its value with near (r = 0.672, p = 0.0006) and far (r = 0.803, p = 6.8e-06) distractors across 22 V4 populations. The driven fractions rest on the 10 populations per area (sessions 3 to 7) where at least one unit's target-alone mean exceeds its blank mean by 1 SD; in the other 12 no unit does (though 8% to 86% of V1 and 23% to 75% of V4 units there exceed the blank mean), so the driven-fraction part is tested on those 10 populations only. The top-unit correlations use all 22. The fraction driven by targets alone is 0.817 (V1) and 0.871 (V4) over the 10 populations, above Figure S6A's range of 0.3 to 0.5; its means over all 22 (0.372 and 0.396) fall in that range only because the 12 populations with no driven unit count as 0. The criterion does not test this fraction.
deviations: Driven fractions computed on the 10 populations per area with any target-driven unit; in the other 12 the blank epochs respond like target epochs.

findings.statement: In sessions 1, 2 and 8 to 11 of the separation file (12 of 22 populations in each area, both animals) the epochs labelled blank (target and distractor contrast 0) and those labelled distractor-only give the same mean counts as the target epochs (mean z against blank -0.18 to 0.16 for target-alone and -0.29 to 0.37 for distractor-only epochs), while in sessions 3 to 7 targets drive the units 1.7 to 3.7 SD above the blank epochs. The labels are aligned with the counts in all sessions (orientation tuning appears with the true labels and not with labels shifted by one epoch), so the blank and distractor-only labels of these six sessions cannot describe what was shown, or their counts are not those epochs'. The contrast parameters hold the same values (0 and 0.5) in every session, so nothing in the labels marks the six sessions; in them 8% to 86% of V1 and 23% to 75% of V4 units have a target-alone mean above their blank mean, against all units in sessions 3 to 7. The spontaneous rate the Methods' selection needs cannot be measured there.

The V1 and V4 entries of each population hold the same number of epochs of every condition but in different orders (the condition agrees at the same index for 3 to 5% of epochs, the level of unrelated orders). The V1 order carries slow fluctuations consistent with recording order (median residual autocorrelation 0.11 at a lag of 10 epochs, 13 of 22 populations above 0.1); the V4 order carries none (0 of 22). The description does not say how epochs are ordered, so V1 and V4 epochs cannot be matched and the even/odd split of V4 cannot follow time. 244 V4 units pass the paper's tuning criterion against its 198, while V1 gives exactly its 146; single random half splits keep 238 and 144 on average, so the order does not explain the difference.

Each column is one stimulus epoch, and each trial had two epochs, but the files do not mark which epochs form a trial or which came first. The orientation experiment's file does not store the distractor spacing. The description mentions neither the blank nor the distractor-only epochs the files hold.

The receptive-field mapping sessions (Figure 1B), the per-session coarse mapping of the target and each distractor (Figure S4) and the waveforms or SNR used for the well-isolated subset are not deposited; three claims cannot be tested.

The verifier read the outputs and re-ran nothing on the real data. Report in transcripts/henry-2022/verifier-2-report.md. It agrees with all 32 outcomes and with the three assumptions.

paper_notes.statement: The data set holds exactly the paper's 396 V1 and 691 V4 units, but the Methods' rule (responses at least 1 SD above spontaneous) applied to them keeps only 115 to 133 V1 and 147 to 174 V4 units, using blank epochs as the spontaneous condition. Figure S6A, which uses the same definition, shows only 0.3 to 0.5 of each population driven. How the deposited units were selected is not documented.
The Results state that the additive term was significantly larger in V4 than in V1 as "t test, p > 0.001", in a sentence that calls the difference significant.

For the paper's authors. (1) How was the spontaneous rate of the selection ("responses at least 1 SD above spontaneous rate") measured, and against which response; the deposited units cannot be regenerated from the blank epochs. (2) The decoders' feature scaling, penalty grid and folds, and the binomial trial count of the threshold-elevation fit, are not given; the threshold elevations here (V1 1.69, V4 7.30 at 1.3 degrees) differ from the reported ones. (3) How the tuning model's means and fit quality were averaged; V1 gives the paper's 146 fitted neurons but m = 0.41 against 0.59. (4) Whether the even/odd reliability used one split in time order; with reliability averaged over random splits V4 keeps 160 neurons, its m and a correlate at r = -0.46 and its simulated V4 slopes are at or below the Figure 2C slopes at only 1 of 4 spacings, so fig5-terms-covary and fig5de-simulated-discriminability rest on the single split; single random splits all give V4 r of -0.64 to -0.89. (5) Under the stated penalty rule, with the grid used here, the chosen decoder has no nonzero coefficient in 5% to 18% of outer folds; whether the paper's did is not said. The analysis code, which the paper offers on request, would settle these.

entries.name: henry-2022
entries.title: Crowding in macaque V1 and V4 populations (Henry and Kohn 2022)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Henry and Kohn (2022) on CRCNS data set v4-2, which holds the spike counts of the V1 and V4 populations recorded in two macaques viewing target gratings alone and amid distractors (11 sessions of the spacing experiment, 4 of the distractor-orientation experiment). It covers single-neuron and population discriminability, threshold elevation, noise correlations, Fano factors, response modulation, the additive and multiplicative tuning model, tuning correlations and fixed decoders. The receptive-field maps and waveforms are not in the data set.
